correctness.rationale: For \(G_{m,n,t}=K_{m,n}-M_t\), a vertex can lose at most one cross-shore neighbor. Therefore three white vertices on either shore are permanently unforceable, reducing the lower bound to a finite set of white-count cases. Separate arguments for \(t=0\), \(t=1\), and \(t\ge2\) give sharp maxima of two, three, and four white vertices, with explicit force chains. The domination exceptions are proved by shore-size obstructions, and explicit one-larger witnesses attain each exceptional bound. Exhaustive replay agrees on 58 connected small profiles and the symbolic witnesses were checked on 681 larger profiles.

value.rationale: The initiating literature treats complete bipartite graphs as a basic exact family for dom-forcing. A deleted matching is the canonical sparse, degree-balanced perturbation of a biclique. The theorem gives a full robustness law across every matching size, proves that the forcing threshold saturates after two deletions, and identifies exactly when domination ceases to be free. This is a natural structural classification rather than a parameter increment or isolated numerical computation.
